# Chezzi — gap backlog

Catch-all backlog of missing / shallow surface. **Not a commitment** — draw from it when a feature
earns its own milestone. Categories: **bugs** (fix, don't backlog), **root causes** (one change that
unblocks many gaps), **language**, **stdlib**, **IO/runtime**, **tooling/ecosystem**, **deps**.

**Audit history:** first stdlib pass 2026-07-07. **Full four-axis audit 2026-07-14** (IO/runtime,
stdlib breadth, language features, tooling) — that pass found one live data-corruption **bug**, three
cross-cutting **root causes** that were each recorded as unrelated footnotes, and a whole missing
**tooling** category. It also found the file's own #1 entry ("number format-specs") had been **shipped
and never de-staled**. Re-audit periodically: a gap backlog nobody re-reads rots into a to-do list for
work already done.

**External dogfood pass 2026-08-17 (`W8-1..W8-20`, the newest and the first NOT run by the people who
built this):** ten developers new to Chezzi, one area each, 343 Chezzi programs checked against 45
reference programs in Python/Go/Rust. It is disjoint from waves 1–7 by construction — those hunted
soundness classes the authors already suspected; this one had no model of the implementation and so found
**silent wrong answers, scheduler defaults, message quality, and stale prose** instead (exactly one
soundness row in twenty). **All twenty were live while every standing gate was green**, which is the
pass's meta-finding — see `## Session log — 2026-08-17`. Closed so far: `W8-18` (doc drift),
`W8-2` (the discarded-carrier warning, 2026-08-17, the latter along with the un-numbered **airlock
trap** section below it), `W8-14` (every runtime stack-trace frame now names its file, 2026-08-17),
`W8-15` (both the `check` and `test` `--errors=json` halves, 2026-08-18), `W8-5` (`json.parse`'s
and `json.stringify`'s depth aborts, 2026-08-18) — the last three all on
`feat/span-file-and-stdlib-contracts` — `W8-6` (`regex.replace_all` rejects Python group refs,
2026-08-27), and `W8-20` (`json.encode`, the `dumps`-shaped inverse of `decode[T]`, 2026-08-28,
TICKET-013). `W8-43` (the shared structural-depth budget across nested
protocol-hook re-entries, 2026-08-18) was found while working this backlog and is filed
already-closed.

**External dogfood pass, wave 2 — 2026-08-18 (`W8-23..W8-42`):** nine independent agents, again with no
model of the implementation, again judging every answer against Python / Go / Rust **run on the same
box**. 30 findings; **27 reproduced in-repo**, and they were filed only after all 15 then-open `W8-*`
rows were re-run and confirmed still live — which is what kept two of them from being filed twice
(they are the same defect as `W8-3` from a different axis, and are folded into that row). Two did NOT
reproduce and are recorded with their measurements rather than filed (a false-`deadlock` shape: 0
failures in 320 runs across two binaries and four worker counts; `io.flush` losing stdout: 0/220).
Four more were filed with their stated shape **corrected** by the re-run. It is disjoint from wave 1
the same way wave 1 is disjoint from waves 1–7: seven of its rows are P0, three of those destroy or
corrupt data (`W8-24` overwrites a user's file, `W8-23` and `W8-35` return confidently wrong numbers),
and **not one of the 30 was reachable by a standing gate** — see `## Session log — 2026-08-18`.

**Pre-freeze bug-hunt waves:** 1–5 (2026-07-11 → 07-13), then 2026-07-18, 07-20, 07-22, three on
07-23, and **wave 7 (2026-07-28)** — batch A swept the **host boundary** (the native/CLI seam where raw
OS bytes become Chezzi values): 3 findings, all FIXED, and it re-confirmed wave 6's meta-finding
(the panicking `std::env::args()` had three call sites, not the one the report named).
**Wave 6 (2026-07-25)** is the largest single haul (**19 findings**) and the first to sweep the two
surfaces the wave-5 residual named as never-audited (FFI: 4 defects; GC + new object layout: clean). As of
2026-07-28 all 19 + the 3 carve-outs are fixed, plus one follow-up found by adversarial review of the

`W6-10r` 2026-08-06). Read its session log
before touching `io`/`process`/FFI/`RwShared`/module-snapshot code. Its meta-finding — **5 of 6 P0s are "a
fix applied to SOME arms of an N-way set"** — is the highest-yield remaining lever. **Wave 7
(2026-07-28)** is running against exactly that lever; `W7-3` (a `recover:` inside a cancelled task's
`defer` was bypassed) and `W7-4` (two sibling closures over one captured local got separate cells across

| ~~**W8-1**~~ | `:236` | **String interpolation silently eats regex quantifiers, and the docs taught the form that breaks.** `p := "\\d{4}-\\d{2}"; print(p)` → `\d4-\d2`; CPython `print("\\d{4}-\\d{2}")` → `\d{4}-\d{2}`. Interpolation is always on, so `{4}` is a hole, not a quantifier — and the result is **still a valid regex** (a digit then a literal `4`), so `regex.find` returns `Ok(None)` for every line and *nothing anywhere reports a problem*. In the reporters' log-analyzer this surfaced as `lines=0 malformed=2010` and was the longest single debugging stretch of the campaign | **DOC HALF DONE 2026-08-17**, code half open. `docs/syntax.md` §10 and `docs/stdlib.md` §`std.regex` now both say *use `r"…"`; in a normal string `{n}` is interpolation* — the drift was that §`std.regex` taught the doubled-backslash normal-string form verbatim while the raw-string advice lived in §10, far from where you are when you write a pattern. Open: the optional **lexer nudge** — warn when an interpolation hole's contents are *entirely digits*, which is never a useful expression and is exactly this bug's signature. Cheap, and it converts a silent corruption into a compile-time nudge **FIXED 2026-08-29 (TICKET-018).** A hole whose whole text is ASCII digits now renders literally instead of interpolating, so `"\\d{4}-\\d{2}"` keeps its quantifiers. |
| ~~**W8-2**~~ | `:236` | **CLOSED 2026-08-17 — a discarded `Result`/`Option` now warns; and the Fix column filed below it was MEASURED WRONG on its top-level half and deliberately not shipped.** As filed: `fn f(): g()` where `g() -> Result[int, Error]` returns `Err("E")` — `chezzi check` said *ok: no type errors*, `chezzi run` printed nothing and exited **0**, while the same `g()` at module top level aborted with `runtime error: unhandled error: E`, rc=1. **What shipped is a WARNING, not an error** — Rust's `unused_must_use` is the governing ancestor because both carriers are `#[must_use]` there and the drop is a *lint*, not a rejection. Measured on the release binary: *warning (line 4, col 5): the Result returned by 'g' is discarded — bind it* `r := g()` *, or discard it explicitly* `_ := g()` — program still runs, rc unchanged, and `check --errors=json` carries `"severity":"warning"` | **CLOSED, and the prescription is the part to read.** The Fix as filed said *"top level becomes a compile error"*, removing the asymmetry. **That is wrong where it would fire, and was not shipped.** Measured, same program, two spellings: bare `g()` at top level → `runtime error (line 3, col 1): unhandled error: E`, **rc=1**; with the escape the warning itself recommends, `_ := g()` → prints `after`, **rc=0**. The runtime already checks a top-level drop (`Op::PopExprStmt` → `top_level_error`, `src/vm/exec.rs`), so "is discarded" is a **factually false** claim in that position and obeying it *disables the only check the program had*. The rule is therefore gated **OFF at module top level** and fires only inside a non-top-level proto that can hold a statement — a `fn` body, a `spawn:` block, a `defer:` block — each measured swallowing at top level. The gate was derived from the RUNTIME, not from a plausible checker flag: an exhaustive walk of the **eight `FnComp::new` sites** in `src/compiler/mod.rs` (only `<toplevel>` sets `is_toplevel`); `if`/`for`/`while`/`match` arm/`parallel:`/`recover:`/`wait:` arm all compile into the *enclosing* proto and were each measured aborting at top level, so all stay silent. **The asymmetry is KEPT and justified, not removed.** Measured non-fires, each pinned by a `no_warn` test: `defer f.close()` and `spawn g()` (call forms — Go's canonical unchecked idioms, see **W7-46**), an inline-expr fn body and a value-block tail (implicit returns, not drops), `?` / `??` (they yield the unwrapped payload). `o()?.len()` **does** warn — optional chaining re-wraps to `int?`. A carrier laundered through a type parameter (`fn drop_it[T](x: T): x`) escapes the rule — measured silent, rc=0 — and **Rust is identical** (`T` carries no `#[must_use]`), so that is an ancestor-aligned limit recorded in `syntax.md` §9, not a residual. Corpus: 11 `_ :=` sites, all in `fn`/`test fn` bodies. Not `W7-48` (the `?`-in-`spawn:` swallow), a different site. **The W8-19 pressure behind this row is untouched and still open:** `Option`/`Result` still have **zero** methods, so every fallback is still a 3-line `match` — fixing W8-19 is what makes W8-2-shaped code rarer, the warning only makes it visible. Docs: `syntax.md` §9 (position table), `spec.md` entry model. **REVERSED 2026-09-02, TICKET-038 — the top-level gate above is deleted; `Op::PopExprStmt`'s top-level abort is gone, so this warning is now the ONLY check on a dropped carrier, and it fires in every position, top level included.** Measured before/after on `fn g() -> Result[int, str]: return Err("boom")` followed by a bare `g()`: was `runtime error (x.chz:3:1): unhandled error: boom`, rc=1; is now the W8-2 warning on stderr plus the following statement's output, rc=**0**. Reason: all three owning ancestors exit 0 on a dropped error value (Rust warns via `#[must_use]`, Go's compiler is silent, Python raises only on `raise`), and the old top-level net was already escaped by both `r := g()` and `_ := g()`, so any binding form defeated it — this warning's own advice (`_ := g()`) used to change the exit code, which is now fixed by removing the runtime check it contradicted. One narrowing accepted, not compensated: a value that only LOOKS like a carrier at run time — a user `enum` with an `Err` variant, shadowing the builtin — while its statement's DECLARED type is not a carrier (e.g. `fn f() -> int: x := Err(5)?; return x` then a bare `f()`) now exits 0 with **no diagnostic at all**, where the old runtime check aborted on it regardless of declared type. Accepted because the warning channel is type-driven by design: the checker has no static reason to look inside a non-carrier return type. |
| ~~**W8-3**~~ | `:236` | **`Shared.set()` inside `Shared.update()` loses the write with no signal, and the docs describe behaviour the runtime does not have.** `docs/stdlib.md` said all reentrancy self-deadlocks. Measured — at the default worker count and again at `CHEZZI_THREADS=2`, identical both times (the reporters saw it at every count they tried) — it does **three** different things: `get` inside `update` **succeeds** returning the PRE-guard value (a stale read); `set` inside `update` is **silently lost, rc=0** (`Shared(10)` + nested `set(99)` under an `update(+1)` ends at **11**); `update` inside `update` / `write` inside `write` **hang forever with no deadlock report**. Same for the `RwShared` analogues; `write` nested in `read` is the one legal crossing (it persists) | Notable because the deadlock detector catches its **three other shapes in milliseconds** with better messages than Go's — this path slips past it, so the hang is the only self-reporting cell and it doesn't report either. **Two fixes, independent:** (a) the lost `set` should fault (`set on a box already write-locked by this task`) rather than be overwritten by the guard's return value — a wrong answer becoming a message; (b) the nested-guard hang should reach the deadlock verdict, which per **`parked-is-not-stuck`** means it must be built from what is *impossible* (this task holds the lock it is waiting on — that IS impossible, so it qualifies) and not from what looks idle. Doc corrected 2026-08-17 with the measured 3-row table. **WIDENED 2026-08-18 (dogfood wave 9) — two more shapes, same root cause, and the filed prescription is re-derived.** The root cause is documented as deliberate: `docs/concurrency.md:598` says `read`/`write` *"copy the value out of the lock and **drop the guard before running the closure**"*, so `update` is not a critical section at all — while `:596`, two lines above, promises *"the whole `write` is serialised so concurrent writers can't lose each other's updates"*. **(a) CROSS-TASK:** `s := Shared(0)`; one task runs `s.update(slow)` (300 ms), another `s.set(100)` at +100 ms → **`s = 1`**, the `set` silently lost, identical at threads 1/2/4; the paired Go mutex program prints **100**. Replacing the sleep with 0.4 s of pure CPU still prints `1`, so it is not a park artifact. **This is where the filed fix (a) is WRONG**: faulting the lost `set` is right for the same-task shape and wrong here, where the clobbering `set` is on another task and a fault would be the **[[parked-is-not-stuck]]** mistake — it must **block**. **(b) CROSS-BOX `update`-in-`update`** (`a.update`'s closure calls `b.update`, and the mirror) **hangs forever** — rc=124 at 1/2/4 threads, no output, no deadlock report — and `docs/concurrency.md:605` blesses that exact program: *"(Re-entering a **different** box, or a same-box `read`/`get`, is fine.)"*. **(c)** the same body as a `test fn` under `chezzi test --timeout=2000` also returns **rc=124** — the runner itself hangs — while the same flag correctly reports `1 timed out` for a spin loop, so a `Shared` lock wait is invisible to the only mechanism that exists for hangs and this shape hangs CI forever. **Ordering constraint that falls out of (b):** today the inversion cannot happen through `get` *because* the guard is dropped, so holding the guard makes (b) MORE reachable — the deadlock verdict in fix (b) must land in the SAME commit as the guard, or the fix converts a silent wrong answer into a new class of hang. Wave-9 session log: `## Session log — 2026-08-18` **CLOSED 2026-08-29 (TICKET-016).** A same-box `set`/`update`/`write` re-entry now faults (`deadlock: this task already holds the update guard on this Shared box`) instead of silently losing the nested write, measured `Shared(10)` + nested `set(99)` under `update(+1)` now `rc=1` with that message instead of `11, rc=0`. A cross-task `set` racing an `update` now **blocks and lands** (`s = 100`, matching Go), via a process-global wait-for-graph update guard (`Vm::acquire_update_guard`/`release_update_guard`) rather than the per-box `update_lock` deadlocking on re-entry; a genuine cross-box wait cycle (`a.update` calling `b.update` while the mirror runs) now faults with `deadlock: two or more tasks each hold a Shared/RwShared update guard the other is waiting for (a lock cycle)` instead of hanging at rc=124, while the identical program with no cycle (a completes before b needs it) still runs to `done`. `get`/`read` stay guard-free (still read the pre-guard value) and `write` nested in `read` still persists. `docs/concurrency.md:596-605` and the `docs/stdlib.md` reentrancy table are corrected to match. |

CPython refuses: `ValueError: list modified during sort`. Same for a `pop()` in the callback | `Vm::sort_mutation_check` compares the live list to the rooted pre-sort snapshot by raw `Value` word immediately before the write-back, at all three sites (`list_sort_by`/`list_sort_by_key` in `src/vm/call.rs`, `list_sort_structs` in `src/vm/arith.rs`); a change now faults with `list modified during '<method>' -- a sort callback must not mutate the list being sorted`, matching CPython |
| ~~**W8-5**~~ | `:236` | **CLOSED 2026-08-18 (task B1, `feat/span-file-and-stdlib-contracts`) — both sites fixed.** As filed: `json.parse` on deeply-nested input kills the process despite its `Result` contract. `"[".repeat(100000) + "]".repeat(100000)` matched with a correct `Ok`/`Err` `match` → `runtime error (line 43, col 9): maximum call depth (10000) exceeded`, rc=1, and the trailing `print("still alive")` **never ran**. Go returns `exceeded max depth` and CPython raises a catchable `RecursionError`; both stay alive. **Re-measured on the release binary, the identical repro** (task C, 2026-08-18): `err: exceeded max depth` then `still alive`, rc=0 — the `Result` contract is now total, no `recover:` needed | `std.json` is recursive-descent **in pure Chezzi**, so nesting depth in attacker-controlled input becomes recursion depth in the program — a caller that correctly matched `Ok`/`Err` used to die anyway, which made this a **crash/DoS on untrusted input**, not a cosmetic gap. **Fix: a `Parser.depth: int` counter, capped at `MAX_NEST_DEPTH = 2000`, returns `Err("exceeded max depth")`** instead of letting the VM's own 10 000-frame call-depth cap abort the process — 2.5× headroom below the measured death point (nesting depth 5000, no surrounding call frames). **SECOND SITE — `json.stringify` had the same defect and no error channel to fix it with — also CLOSED.** `stringify(j) -> str` can't return an `Err`, so it stays a **fault** past the same 2000-depth cap, but now named (`json.stringify: exceeded max depth`, via a `stringify_depth(j, depth)` inner helper) and recoverable under `recover:` — re-measured (task C): under `recover:` gives `Err`, message names itself, process stays alive; uncaught it still faults (rc=1) with a filed, named stack trace, the same shape CPython's `json.dumps` uses (`RecursionError`, itself only catchable via `try`/`except`, not silent). Both documented at `docs/stdlib.md:1729-1748`. ~~`json.get` and `json.len` are self-recursive too (verified in source) and share the class.~~ **CORRECTION (task B1, 2026-08-18): false.** Both are flat single-`match` functions — neither calls itself; only `stringify` and the two `Parser` container arms ever recursed. Frames now name their file too (**W8-14**, closed the same branch). **Also found in task B1, not a bug: `stringify` has a SECOND, unrelated fault — a `Json.Num` holding NaN/±inf → `cannot serialize non-finite float to JSON`.** CPython's `json.dumps` emits a bare `NaN` (invalid JSON); Go's `encoding/json` returns `json: unsupported value: NaN`. Chezzi is right to refuse — a written contract (task B2), not a fix |
| ~~**W8-6**~~ | `:236` | **CLOSED 2026-08-27 — `replace_all` now returns an `Err` naming `$N`.** **`regex.replace_all` with Python's `\1` silently emits literal backslashes.** `replace_all(r"(\d+)-(\d+)", "10-20", r"$2/$1")` → `Ok('20/10')`; the same call with `r"\2/\1"` → `Ok('\\2/\\1')`. No error, `Ok`, plausible-looking output. The dialect is **RE2 (the Rust `regex` crate)** and replacement is `$1`/`${name}`, but the docs named no dialect at all | **Filed as the SIXTH silent wrong answer, not a doc row** — same shape as **W8-1** (plausible value, rc=0, Python muscle memory, no diagnostic), and the two share one fix seam: validate the *replacement template* the way a pattern is validated. A `\<digit>` in a replacement string has no meaning in RE2, so rejecting it (or accepting it as an alias for `$<digit>`) is safe and total. | ~~**W8-43**~~ | `:236` | **FIXED 2026-08-18 — checker-clean pure Chezzi could kill the process by host stack overflow, uncatchable by `recover:`, because a user `eq`/`str` hook re-entered the native structural walker with a FRESH depth-0 budget.** Neither guard could fire: call depth stayed far below its 10 000 cap while the *product* of hook-nesting depth × per-hook walk depth grew unbounded. Measured on the pre-fix release binary — a `Leaf.eq` that compares two freshly-built 100-link chains, nested 5 000 deep: `fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting`, **rc=134, core dumped**, and the `print("still alive")` after the `recover:` NEVER ran. CPython 3.14 on the same shape gives a catchable `RecursionError: Stack overflow (used 8148 kB) in comparison` — rc=0, process alive; Python is the owning ancestor for protocol semantics and its model is ONE recursion budget shared across nested re-entries. The defect **defeated the stated contract of the constant itself** (`src/vm/mod.rs`: this bound "turns that into a recoverable `RuntimeError`") and was **documented as deliberate in two source comments** — `values_equal_guarded`'s "starts a FRESH depth-0 walk … bounded there by the call-depth guard" and `stringify_into`'s "a `str` method re-stringifies at the *same* depth" — which is why no review ever questioned it. **No standing gate could reach it**: a SIGABRT has no assertion to fail, and while the CPython differential has classified signal-kills as findings since W7-33, `src/difftest/generate.rs` has no user-struct-with-protocol-method feature, so a hook-nested walk is structurally outside its corpus | **Fix: one shared budget.** New `Vm::walk_base` (per-`Vm`, beside `native_reentry` and for the identical reason — a fiber cannot park while a native re-entry is on the host stack, so no other fiber can observe it) holds the depth the enclosing walks already consumed; all **7** `MAX_STRUCTURAL_DEPTH` comparisons now test `walk_base + depth`, and the **4** `run_proto` dispatch sites that have a live structural `depth` in scope (the `eq` hook, and the `str` hook's struct/enum/newtype arms) go through a new panic-safe `Vm::guarded_walk`. The `catch_unwind` in that helper is load-bearing: `guarded` resumes an unwind from inside itself, so a plain post-call restore would leak `walk_base` onto a shell `Vm` that `run_one_fiber` keeps alive for the NEXT fiber. The cheaper alternative — charge `depth` to `call_depth` around each hook — was rejected because `GenCtx` carries its own `call_depth` and the generator resume swaps it away. Post-fix the repro prints `still alive` at **rc=0** with a recoverable `maximum structural depth (10000) exceeded`. Not charged: `hash`/`struct_compare` (O(1) native frames per `run_proto` — already `MAX_CALL_DEPTH`'s job) and `msort_indices_structs` (O(log n) frames per call level; ceiling recorded in a `ponytail:` comment beside the recursion). **CORRECTED 2026-08-18 (adversarial review, finding B1) — charging two of the seven guards was itself a silent wrong answer, and has been reverted.** Two guards do not fault, they DEGRADE: `cyclic_walk` (`src/vm/arith.rs:1415`) returns `true` (store the map/set key by reference) and `snapshot_value` (`:1477`) aliases the tail. The first cut charged `walk_base` to both and defended it as "the correct stack-safety direction"; it is not. **Charging a guard whose over-budget branch DEGRADES rather than FAULTS converts a stack-safety measure into a silent wrong value**, because an ORDINARY, shallow, acyclic key is pushed into the degrade branch merely because it was inserted from inside an `eq`/`str` hook running at depth — the key is then stored by reference, and the caller's later mutation reaches the stored key with no fault to show for it. Measured on the branch binary, one nesting level apart (`eq` hook inserts `k := K([1])` into `{k: 1}`, mutates `k`, reads the stored key back): depth 4998 → `true`, depth 4999 → **`false`**; pre-branch it is `true` at every depth. **The rule that survives: only a FAULTING guard may share the budget.** Both are back on the bare `depth` (which is also pre-branch semantics exactly, so the revert cannot introduce anything), and they stay charged IDENTICALLY to each other so `store_key_by_reference` and `snapshot_key` agree on which keys are over-deep. Their host-stack exposure at that seam is pre-existing and out of this row's scope. Pinned by `tests/chz/spec/eq_protocol_containers_test.chz::key_inserted_from_a_deep_eq_hook_is_still_snapshotted` at both depths |

The arg-side gate moved out of `check_args_range_decl` into `Checker::constrain_empty_arg` and is now called from `infer_generic_call`/`infer_generic_method` too, at the last moment `subst_map` can change — neither generic path routes through `check_args*`, which is the whole of route 2. **The arg gate had to TIGHTEN from `!contains_unknown_in_slot` to `ty_fully_concrete`:** a substituted generic slot can still be `List[T]` with `T` free, and `Ty::Param` is not `Ty::Unknown`, so the first cut pinned the binding to a rigid `List[T]` and reported *expected T, found int* on `fn ident[T](xs: List[T])` — a program that must pin nothing. Caught by the existing `ok()` neighbour, which is why that neighbour was written. **Route 1's fix is a DELETION, and the plausible repair was measured wrong.** Snapshotting `empty_coll_sites` alongside the binding types does NOT fix the value arm — it just forgets the constraining use entirely and lets the later push win (measured: still `['a', 1]`). The barrier itself was the defect: `snapshot_refinable`/`restore_refinable` are **deleted**, and a value-arm pin now persists exactly like statement position, which is what `docs/syntax.md`'s scope-wide rule already promised everywhere else. A value arm is a single expression, so the only refinement reachable inside one is `constrain_empty_arg` — `push`/`add` and `m[k]=v` are statements and cannot appear there — which is why the barrier had so little left to protect. **Neighbour table for that narrowing, run on the pre-fix binary** (both newly-rejected rows were `ok: no type errors` before): two CONFLICTING concrete uses across sibling value arms reject, in the `if` spelling, the `match` spelling and for a `Map` binding — the same rule two conflicting pushes already follow, and the one Rust applies (a `Vec` cannot be both `Vec<String>` and `Vec<i32>`); AGREEING arms, an arm-only use, and an arm followed by a CONSISTENT later use all still check clean and run. **CEILING, measured and deliberately not closed — the un-annotated ALIAS.** `b := []` / `c := b` / `c.push(1)` / `b.push("a")` prints `[1, 'a']`, unchanged by all of the above: `c := b` has no concrete sink to pin from, so the requirement legitimately MOVES to `c` (the documented escape rule) and the two names are then pinned independently while sharing one runtime list. Closing it needs alias-identity tracking, which would newly REJECT a rebound alias (`c := b` then `c = [1, 2]` then `b.push("a")`) — a false rejection is worse than this missing one, and neither ancestor settles it: Rust forbids the shape outright (`let c = b` MOVES), Python has no static element type at all. Recorded in `docs/syntax.md` as the one remaining sliver, replacing the value-arm sliver this row closed. Pinned by `every_constraining_use_pins_the_element_type` (all seven routes, the alias ceiling and its annotation escape) and `a_value_arm_pin_persists_like_statement_position` (the narrowing's full neighbour table). **ADVERSARIAL REVIEW (2 prosecutors) on the shipped commit found 3 real defects, all fixed, and re-scoped a fourth.** (a) **FALSE REJECTION, high, FIXED.** The pin's BINDING gate was the broad `contains_unknown_in_slot`, which also matches `Option[Unknown]` (`o := None`) and a nullary generic enum variant (`e := Box.Empty`) — values that record no site, ask for no annotation, and must stay permissive. Measured: `e := Box.Empty` / `a: Box[int] = e` / `b: Box[str] = e` went from running to *cannot assign Box[int] to variable of type Box[str]*, and the `None` twin the same. Fixed by cutting on `is_unrefined_empty_coll` — **the identical mistake W8-45(a) made in the opposite direction**, and the identical repair: the gate must be the shape the receiving machinery handles, never a superset that looks related. The fix also closes the same false rejection on the ARGUMENT path, where the wide gate was PRE-EXISTING (measured rejected on both binaries before). (b) **ORDER DEPENDENCE, critical, FIXED.** The assignment arm's target-type probe was gated on `empty_coll_sites.is_empty()` — written as a perf shortcut, but it decides whether the assignment PINS, so acceptance depended on an unrelated binding elsewhere in the file. Measured, two programs differing only in where an unrelated `z.push(1)` sits: before the assignment rc=0, after it *cannot assign Option[str] to variable of type Option[int]* rc=1. Now gated on `escapes_unrefined_empty(value)` — a property of THAT statement alone. (c) **A FALSE JUSTIFYING CLAIM, FIXED.** The barrier-removal note said `push`/`add` "are statements and cannot appear" in a value arm; `y := if c: xs.push(1) else: xs.push("a")` parses and does reach `refine_receiver`. It returns nil, so such a program is rejected either way — the removal changes which diagnostic it gets, not whether it is accepted — but the note was the sole stated justification and was simply wrong. (d) **RE-SCOPED, not fixed, by measurement.** The pin does not re-run `refine_receiver`'s `Hashable` ban, so `s := Set()` / `c: Set[float] = s` / `s.add(1.5)` loses one of its three errors. Run across every shape that can reach it (annotated sink, typed parameter, typed return), an illegal `Set[float]` cannot be SPELLED without erroring at the spelling site — the fact is always still reported (twice, at the annotation), so what is lost is a THIRD copy, never the only one. Restoring it would print the same fact three times; recorded instead, with a test pinning that the program stays rejected. **The alias ceiling was also understated and is now documented honestly:** it is not a benign mixed print — the two static types disagree about a shared value, so `fn addstr(xs: List[str]) -> str: return xs[0].upper()` called on the unpinned half is `ok: no type errors` and then *type int has no method 'upper'* at run time. `docs/syntax.md` carries that repro, the annotation escape that closes it, and the reason the checker fix is refused. A new `(scope, name)`-keyed `empty_coll_aliases` pin group (drained at `pop_scope`, untainted at `declare`, unlinked in `check_assign`'s funnel) propagates a pin across the pair; a whole-binding reassignment or re-declaration of either name still breaks it, so a rebound alias is never falsely rejected. |
| ~~**W8-47**~~ | W8-44 review | **CLOSED 2026-09-02 — a non-inline default whose slot type mentioned a type parameter made that parameter/field non-omittable even when a turbofish had already pinned the binder, and the filed root cause was measured FALSE.** As filed: `struct Holder[T]: n: int; items: List[G[T]] = mkl()` (on `fn mkl[Z]() -> List[G[Z]]`) then `Holder(1)` reports *Holder() expects 2 argument(s), got 1*. Two SEPARATE mechanisms, not one: a **free fn** (`fn conv[T](a: int, b: List[T] = mkl())`) is rejected by an exact arity test in `infer_generic_call` (`args.len() != sig.params.len()`), while `FnSig::min_params`/`ast::min_callable_params` already computes the shrunk count and every non-generic path already uses it. A **struct ctor** has a different cause: `desugar::dflt_for` returns `Dflt::CalleeFilled` for the field, `normalize_call` omits the argument (correct for a fn, which has a callee prologue to fill it from), but `Op::NewStruct` takes its field count from the CALL SITE, so the ctor call is genuinely short by one argument and the checker's own arity check (correctly) refuses it. The filed root cause — `min_callable_params` counting a defaulted trailing param as required, the message coming from `check_args_range_decl` — was measured FALSE on both counts | **Fix, two independent commits.** **Free fn:** `infer_generic_call`'s gate is now `!(sig.min_params..=sig.params.len()).contains(&args.len())`; a witness-taking callee (`fn conv[T: Default](a: int, b: List[T] = List())`, body calling `T.default()`) keeps its full arity because `min_callable_params` returns `params.len()` whenever the sig carries witness params — pinned by `w8_47_a_witness_taking_callee_keeps_its_full_arity` beside the pre-existing `witness_forwarding_still_charges_every_unpinned_shape_rejected`. Before/after: `conv[int](1)` and `conv(1)` both go from *conv() expects 2 argument(s), got 1* to `ok: no type errors` (witness-free); the witness-taking shape stays rejected. **Struct ctor: the arity check is NOT lifted** — a ctor has no callee, so `desugar` no longer leaves one short when the turbofish is complete instead. New `Dflt::GenericProvider`: a field default whose type mentions the struct's own UNBOUNDED type parameters gets a provider generic in those parameters, and the ctor's own turbofish is FORWARDED to it (`normalize_call` declines the splice when the counts don't match, keeping today's short call). Before/after: `Holder[int](1)` goes from *Holder() expects 2 argument(s), got 1* to `ok`, prints `1` then `0`. `Holder(1)` (no turbofish to forward) now reports the W8-45-style *cannot infer type parameter T for 'Holder'; the default for field 'items' can only be filled with explicit type arguments, e.g. Holder[int](...)* — matching Rust's `error[E0282]: type annotations needed for Holder<_>` on the same shape — needed a new `StructInfo.defaulted_fields` so the checker can tell an omitted DEFAULTED field from a missing required one. **Residual, measured and accepted:** a BOUNDED owner type parameter (`struct Holder[T: Show]`) keeps the plain arity refusal even with a turbofish written — a generic provider carrying the bound would raise a witness question `dflt_for` cannot answer before types exist, and "add explicit type arguments" would be FALSE advice there since the turbofish is already present. **Widening, measured and covered:** giving a generic field a provider means the provider BODY is now judged for a `?` in the default (DEC-025), which the field decl-site copy never did — `items: List[G[T]] = mkl()?` on a `!str`-returning `mkl` went from `ok: no type errors` to *a default expression cannot propagate with `?`*. **Test-helper gotcha:** `ok()`/`check_src` skips `desugar` entirely, so the committed ctor test (`w8_47_struct_ctor_default_arity_is_binder_blind`) moved to `ok_desugared` — under `check_src` every defaulted field is unfilled regardless of the fix |

The circularity was in the coarse predicate, not in the idea. **Two high-severity defects caught by adversarial review** (three prosecutors, two converging independently), both reproduced before acceptance: (1) **the judge was EDGE-triggered** — after judging it parked in an untimed `cv.wait`, and nothing notifies a sched when a *party registers*, so a verdict that became true later was never asked (**5/5 deterministic hangs** on two repros; the tell was that adding a third job whose `finish` pokes the sched made the same program fault). (3) a memory-ordering claim that did not hold — an `Acquire` load orders only *subsequent* reads and `jump_checked` reads cancel *before* exit, so the publication order never guaranteed the rung order; the claim is deleted, not softened. **Also closed, the asymmetry this change itself created:** `Vm::guarded` gained an exit rung but had no deadline rung, so `chezzi test --timeout=500` reported **`PASS` on a native-HOF test that ran 1985 ms** — a cap silently not applying, which teaches distrust of every green run. `guarded` now runs `deadline → cancel → exit`, matching `jump_checked`. **Perf:** the rung had to go in a `#[cold] #[inline(never)]` helper — inlined it cost **+4.5% on `loop.chz`, a bench that never calls `guarded` at all** (pure code-layout perturbation, isolated by deleting exactly those lines). Final independent A/B (hyperfine, 20 runs): `loop` +1.0%, `list` +1.0%, and **`fib` — the zero-loop control the rung cannot touch — also +1.2%**, so the movement is layout noise, not the change. **A measured limit of the constraints, now DOCUMENTED and made honest rather than filed:** a fiber inside an offloaded **blocking-pool** native (`process.cmd("sleep 5")`) is in a libc call whose only checkpoint is at entry. Measured identical for all three halts — sibling fault/cancel 5013 ms, `os.exit` 5015 ms, `--timeout=500` 5008 ms — so it is **not exit-specific**, and it is the deliberate price of offloading these calls so they never pin a core worker. Reaching it needs a signal, an fd close, or `process::exit`, and `stream.rs:17-20` refuses the last for documented reasons. Two things were done about it instead of a follow-up row (2026-08-12): (1) **`docs/stdlib.md` now documents it** — a shared *"Blocking calls cannot be interrupted"* section covering the `std.io` file seams, every `std.fs` syscall, every `std.process` runner and every `std.request` call, linked from all four module sections plus `std.cancel` (which advertises "cooperative cancellation & timeouts" and would otherwise mislead), telling the reader to bound the operation itself. (2) **the cap stopped lying**: `chezzi test --timeout=300` reported **`PASS`** on a test that ran 5008 ms; a post-hoc check in `test_runner.rs` now upgrades an over-cap `Pass` to `TIMED-OUT` with a message that distinguishes it from a real abort (*"…ran 3002ms and could not be aborted…"*), and only `Pass` is upgraded — a `Fail`/`Error`/`OverMemory` keeps its more informative bucket. Verified: verdict, summary counts, `--fail-fast`, the quiet renderer, the JSON status and **exit 1** all treat it as a real timeout |

Fixed in the two places the shape is decided, NOT by special-casing the message: the checker's receiver sweep (`sig.rs`) skips exactly `Ty::Module`, and `Compiler::receiverless_call_head` now answers yes for a module head too, so the call is replayed through the wrapper proto its eager spelling emits instead of pushing the module HANDLE as a `SpawnMethod` receiver. **Both legs were needed** — the checker-only cut traded the check error for a *"this task value can't cross a worker boundary … a module handle cannot cross"* runtime fault (the checker-superset-of-compiler class). **Real sendability is NOT weakened:** the skip is keyed on an UNBOUND MODULE NAME — the same two clauses `receiverless_call_head` lowers on, so check-time and lowering cannot disagree — so a container merely holding a module (`xs := [math]` → `spawn xs.clear()` → *"cannot spawn on a non-sendable receiver of type List[module math]"*), a local that SHADOWS a module name (`math := [math]`, same message), a local BOUND to the module (`m := math` → `spawn m.abs(-3)` → *"cannot spawn on a non-sendable receiver of type module math"*), and every non-sendable ARGUMENT (`spawn take(math)` → *"cannot pass a non-sendable value of type module math to a spawned task"*) are refused with byte-identical messages before and after. **Keying it on the RESOLVED `Ty::Module` instead was itself a regression, fixed 2026-08-15:** a module bound to a local is `Ty::Module` but not a namespace head, so `chezzi check` said *ok: no type errors* and `chezzi run` faulted with *"a module handle cannot cross"* — the checker-superset-of-compiler class, one commit after the fix that introduced it (`checker::tests::spawn_on_non_sendable_receiver_still_rejected` now pins both bound spellings). Cover: `checker::tests::spawn_on_module_qualified_fn_ok` + `spawn_on_non_sendable_receiver_still_rejected` + `spawn_non_sendable_argument_still_rejected` + the flipped `witness_fn_is_a_cross_module_defer_target_ok`, and 4 `test fn`s in `tests/chz/spec/spawn_module_target_test.chz` (user module, aliased import, bare `spawn` with no nursery, native module — each asserting the spawned call's OBSERVABLE effect, both engines) | — |
| ~~**M24-6**~~ | `Diagnostics / spans` | **FIXED 2026-08-11 — an interpolation fragment's reported position is now the fragment's REAL physical source position, line and column, at any nesting depth.** Mechanism: the lexer builds a per-literal sparse checkpoint map (`PosMap`, content-char index → source `Span`) and hangs it on the `str` token (`Token::Str(StrLit { raw, map })`); a fragment is re-lexed by `lexer::tokenize_frag(src, map, off)`, whose `span_at` asks the map instead of counting columns. **One rule builds it: `note(idx, at)` records a position only when it is NOT what the previous checkpoint already implies** — called per content char at the top of `string()`/`triple_string()`, with no case analysis over escape kinds. Per-char is load-bearing, not tidiness: a literal nested inside a fragment builds its own map out of `span_at`, i.e. out of the PARENT's map, so a parent `\t`/`\u{…}` escape's column jump is invisible to the inner lexer and any "record at escapes and newlines" shortcut would put the inner fragment one column left of the truth. Measured, `chezzi run`/`check`, pre-change binary vs post-change: `s := """aaa\nbbb\ncc {10 / z} dd"""` (real newlines) **(2,19) → (4,5)**; the same literal with `\n` ESCAPES **(2,19) → (2,21)**; `print("{ f('a\tb{nope}c') }")` on line 3 **(3,17) → (3,18)**. The first two are the punchline: they were the SAME wrong answer, because `raw` is the post-escape payload and the old design could not tell a real newline from a `\n` escape. The `"""`-short-by-2 and per-escape drifts disappear for free — checkpoint 0 is taken on entry to `string()`/`triple_string()`, where `self.pos` already sits past the opening delimiter. Cost, stated exactly (adversarial review caught the first cut claiming more than it delivered — `PosMap::flat` used to `vec![]` unconditionally, so a brace-free literal of 2M `\t` escapes built and dropped **43 MB**, measured by peak RSS): checkpoint 0 is held INLINE on the map, so a literal with no escapes and no newlines leaves `pts` empty and an empty `Vec` does not heap-allocate — the common case is genuinely free. A literal WITH escapes pushes one checkpoint per discontinuity, and `map` is kept only if the literal contains `{` or `}` (the same guard desugar uses), so a brace-free escape-heavy literal still builds a small `Vec` and drops it — work proportional to escapes, not to length, and avoidable only with a second escape-aware pre-scan (`ponytail:` noted at the call site, not worth it until a profile says so). `raw`/`RawStr`/`Bytes` scanners get no map at all. `StrLit`'s `Debug` is hand-written to print as the bare `String`, so `chezzi tokens` / `chezzi ast` output is byte-identical — a derived `Debug` had turned one interpolated literal into a screenful of `Span` blocks (also adversarial review). Runtime-inert — the `.chz` suite is green on both engines. **Retractions of this row's own claims.** (a) "Exact positions are not recoverable here" — they are; `raw` is lossy but the LEXER is not, and recording as it scans costs a `Vec` of a handful of checkpoints. (b) The cost estimate "changes `Token::Str`, the AST node and every match site" — actual: **2 real parser edits** (`expect_str`, the pattern-literal arm, both splitting a `Token::Str | Token::RawStr` or-pattern), **3 signature-only** (`check_interpolation`, `compile_str`, `interp_exprs`), **~12 zero-edit sites** (`Deref<Target = str>` covers `raw.contains('{')` and friends), and ~22 mechanical `"…".to_string()` → `"…".into()` test literals. (c) The predicted true position "line 4, col 8" is wrong for this codebase: a binary expression's span anchors on its LEFT operand, so `10 / z` reports the `1` — **col 5**, verified against the equivalent plain (non-interpolated) program | **The invariant got STRONGER, which is why this was worth doing at all.** `PosMap::at` is injective on a literal's content range: checkpoints are `span_at` at strictly increasing `self.pos` (so distinct, increasing physical positions), and between two checkpoints `note` fired and DECLINED, which is exactly the statement that the run is a contiguous strictly-increasing column range on one line. So a fragment token's span is the true position of a real source char, and `WitnessTable`/`KeywordTable`/`CarrierTable` keys are injective by a property of the FILE rather than of an offset arithmetic we chose. The four hazards check out: two fragments of one literal occupy disjoint `raw` sub-ranges; a nested literal sits physically inside its parent's extent at a strictly later position (the `static_witness_test.chz` sibling collision becomes unrepresentable); there are no zero-width escapes (`\` + newline is a `LexError`); `{{`/`}}` are consumed as content, so a fragment's `raw` index stays true. That retires `2a27697e`'s trade — it bought non-aliasing with a monotone OFFSET that could run off the end of its physical line; this buys it outright. **Cross-ref `W7-49`**, which made the same move for module identity (a `Span` grew a `file` id instead of hoping spans would not repeat across modules): both replace "an encoding we believe is injective" with "the thing itself". Residual, filed and since **FIXED** (2026-08-14, next row): **M24-7** (`LexError` carried no column) **Class cross-ref (2026-08-16): a FOURTH instance of the span-keyed side-table aliasing class landed and was fixed — see the `span-keyed side table, instance #4` row. The class now reads M24-6 / W7-49 / W7-43 / ListWidenTable, and every fix made the coordinate REAL rather than re-anchoring a span.** |
| ~~**M24-7**~~ | `Diagnostics / spans` | **FIXED 2026-08-14 — a lex error points at the offending CHARACTER, on both axes, like every other diagnostic in the compiler.** Measured `chezzi check`, before → after: `z := "ab\u{12zz}cd"` on line 3 — *resolve error (line 3, col 1): lex error (line 3): invalid hex digit in unicode escape* → *resolve error (line 3, col 14): lex error (line 3, col 14): …* (the first `z` of `12zz`); `y := 0x` on line 2 — *(line 2, col 1) / lex error (line 2)* → *(line 2, col 6)* (the `0`); `y := "a\qb"` on line 2 — *(line 2, col 1)* → *(line 2, col 9)* (the `q`); `y := "abc` on line 2 of a 2-line file — *resolve error (line 3, col 1): lex error (line 3): unterminated string literal* → *(line 2, col 6)* (the opening quote), which also fixes the **LINE**: the cursor had run to EOF, so the position was read off the line the FILE ends on. **The position rule** (measured against the ancestors 2026-08-14, rustc 1.x + CPython 3.14; a malformed number → **the start of the numeric literal** (rustc `num.rs:2:13`), **except a misplaced `'_'` group separator, which points at the offending `_`** — CPython 3.14.6 measured: `y = 1__0` → *lineno 2 offset 6*, its first `_`, and `y = 0b1__0` → offset 8, likewise; **rustc has no opinion on this one, it ACCEPTS `1__0` silently** (measured 1.97.0, compiles clean — an earlier note here citing a rustc caret on the doubled underscore was wrong); an unterminated string/triple-string/byte-string → **the OPENING delimiter** (rustc `unterm.rs:2:13`, CPython puts its caret under the opening quote); everything else → the character the message is about. One line: *point at the offending character; an unterminated delimiter points at its opener.* **Where the whole-escape sub-family diverges from rustc, by 1-2 columns and deliberately:** measured rustc 1.97.0, `"x\uZ"` (incorrect escape), `"y\u{}"` (empty), a 7-hex-digit body (overlong) and `"w\u{D800}"` (surrogate) *all* anchor at the `\` and caret-**span** the whole escape; `LexError` carries a point, not a span, so Chezzi names a char *inside* the escape instead — the offending char where there is one (the `Z`, the 7th digit) and otherwise the `{`. Every one is a real character on the right line inside the construct the message is about, which is the bar ("never a confidently wrong column"); matching rustc's anchor exactly needs a span, not a column, so the code was left alone. | Mechanism: `LexError` gained `pub col: usize`, its `Display` is now `lex error (line {}, col {}): {}` (matching `impl Display for Span`), and the seam at `src/resolver/mod.rs:~691` reads `e.col` instead of the hardcoded `col: 1` — so the LSP squiggle, `--errors=json` and the plain-text rendering all land on the bad char with no edit of their own. `Lexer::error` stays the only constructor path, now a three-step funnel: `error()` → `error_at(pos)` → `error_span(span)`, with `error_at` asking `span_at` (which composes through the M24-6 per-literal `PosMap`, so a column inside a re-lexed interpolation fragment is right for free). All 35 construction sites were audited and moved to the position their family calls for. `error_span` exists because `span_at` derives the column as `pos - self.line_start` — it CANNOT recover a position on an earlier line, and an unterminated literal's opener usually is one; the six literal scanners capture their opener's `Span` at entry instead. `Span` itself is untouched (still 12 bytes). **Follow-up fix, same phase:** the string-**interpolation** seam was still throwing the new column away — `interpolation::parse_expr_str` built its `InterpError` from the *string literal's* span, so `s := "a\tb{1 + @}c"` on line 2 rendered *type error (line 2, col 6): lex error (line 2, col 16): unexpected character '@'*: the inner text named the `@`, the OUTER position (the one the LSP squiggles and `--errors=json` emits) named the opening quote. Pinned by `a_lex_error_inside_a_fragment_reports_its_real_line`, which now asserts the OUTER `e.span`. **The PRIMARY path kept stuttering for one more day and is now consistent with it (2026-08-15):** `resolver::parse` still built its message from `LexError::to_string()`, so a module-graph lex error rendered *resolve error (line 1, col 8): in module 'dtest.badmod': lex error (line 1, col 8): unexpected character '@'* — the same position twice, once from the outer renderer and once from the inner `Display`. It now uses `e.message` under the same `lex error: ` prefix the interpolation seam uses. One seam, one rendering rule (`tests/check_errors_json.rs::lex_error_carries_a_real_column` asserts the whole line). **Second follow-up, 2026-08-14 — the seam's remaining four discards, closed:** the lex arm was one of *five* error paths out of `interpolation::parse_interpolation` and the other four all still reported the literal's opening quote. (2) **Unterminated `{`** — `s := "a\tb{1 + c"` → col 6 → **col 17**, the literal's closing delimiter (`map.at(raw.chars().count())`); CPython measured *offset 17*, the same char. Pinned by `checker::tests::a_parse_error_inside_a_fragment_reports_the_fragments_own_position` and `literal_shape_errors_point_at_their_own_char`, both carrying a real `\t` escape before the offending char so a column counted off the post-escape content rather than composed through the `PosMap` lands one to the left and fails. |
| ~~**W7-50**~~ | `Parser / LSP` | **FIXED 2026-08-13 — the two parser depth constants are re-derived from a measurement, the LSP's last unwrapped front-end entry point is on the big stack, and the margin is now an assertion instead of a prose claim.** As filed: `MAX_DEPTH = 64` had **one level** of margin (65 passes, 66 aborts on a ~2 MiB thread) and `editor::semantic_tokens` reached `parser::parse` on the LSP's own ~2 MiB tokio worker. **Half (b), the cheap one, landed first**: `semantic_tokens` hops onto `crate::on_frontend_stack` like `diagnostics`/`hover`, and `cmd_ast`'s `{:#?}` walk with it (`src/editor/mod.rs`, `src/main.rs:~133`) — so no production parse runs on a small stack any more, which is what let `MAX_DEPTH` rise at all. **Half (a) is a re-derivation, not a bump.** An `--ignored` probe (`checker::tests::stack_probe_frontend_walker_depth`) measures the two resources separately, debug build: parse recursion costs **7 753 B per `MAX_DEPTH` unit**, and the binding post-parse walker is `compile` at **12 162 B per AST node** (`desugar` 11 323, `check` 6 850). Against the SMALLER of the two big stacks — `vm::VM_STACK_BYTES` = 384 MiB, which `chezzi run` re-does `build_graph`+`compile_graph` on — that is ~51 900 depth units and ~33 100 AST nodes of budget. **One constant was being asked to bound two resources**, which is why no single value could reach CPython parity. Split: **`MAX_DEPTH` = 64 → 512** (parse recursion only; ~4 MB of 384 MiB, a **~100× margin**), and **`MAX_CHAIN_DEPTH` (500, per-loop) → `MAX_AST_DEPTH` = 16 000** (AST depth). **Measured before/after, release binary, vs CPython 3.14's own limit of 200:** parens **30 → 254**, nested lists **31 → 255**, nested calls **30 → 254**, nested `if` blocks **61 → 509** (CPython 99), unary **61 → 509**, generic types **62 → 510**, match patterns **60 → 508**; the multiplicative `f(g(…).f×498)` fixture **15 → 31**; the double-fold `( … .f×499 +1×499 )` shape **30 → 16**, the one form that NARROWS (see correction 2). **Three corrections the work turned up.** (1) **Parentheses build no AST node** (`parse_primary`'s grouped arm is `return Ok(first)`), so paren nesting spends parse recursion only — which is what makes the split legitimate rather than a loosening. (2) **`MAX_AST_DEPTH` = 16 000 is a DELIBERATE NARROWING of what parses — the first writeup of this row claimed the opposite and was wrong.** The claim was that 16 000 sits above the deepest AST the parser accepted before it existed ("30 nested parens × a 500-fold chain each = 15 000, so nothing that parsed then stops parsing"). That counted only the paren+**infix** shape. A paren level can spend **both** fold loops — `parse_postfix`'s and `parse_bp`'s — for **~998** nodes per level, not 499. **Re-measured 2026-08-13, release binaries, bisected, source `x := ` + *k* × `( … .f×499 +1×499 )`:** `b1307258` accepts *k* = **30** (~**29 940** nodes) and rejects 31; HEAD accepts *k* = **16** (~**15 968** nodes) and rejects 17. So programs between ~16 000 and ~30 000 nodes deep that parsed before now get a clean `expression nested too deeply` — machine-generated code is exactly where those live. **Narrowing was the right call, and it makes the change look better, not worse:** against the measured ~33 100-node cliff the old ceiling had **1.11×** headroom — the parser was accepting programs within ~10% of an uncatchable host SIGABRT on a well-typed program, which is the failure this very row exists to prevent — where 16 000 has **2.07×**. A diagnostic is recoverable; an abort is not. (The `lib.rs` estimate `64 × 500 ≈ 32 k` this correction was originally aimed at turns out to have been very nearly RIGHT at ~29 940; the 7 500 figure was the multiplicative fixture's ceiling only, and 15 000 the single-fold paren shape's — both undercounts of the worst shape.) Buying the depth back needs a bigger `vm::VM_STACK_BYTES`, reserved **per M:N pool worker** — not a bigger constant. Pinned by `parser::tests::deep_iterative_chains_error_not_crash`'s double-fold case (which bisects the single-fold and double-fold shapes and asserts the ratio, so the mechanism is measured rather than re-guessed) and `parser::tests::max_ast_depth_floor_holds` (a FIXED fixture, not derived from the constant, so a silent shrink fails a test). (3) **`chezzi ast` was a latent, not live, crash path** — the `{:#?}` walk was unwrapped, but nothing that parsed could reach a depth that overflowed it. **The design the plan specified was UNSOUND and was replaced with evidence.** The plan bounded `self.depth + chain_total` with `chain_total` an *ambient* per-path fold count decremented on loop exit. A fold loop runs AFTER the descent it sits above, so in `f(g(DEEP) + 1 + 1 + …)` the folds are counted only once `DEEP` has popped its own counts — the two never coexist. **Measured on a probe build with `MAX_DEPTH = 512` and an 8 000 chain ceiling: that shape parses at 45 000 nodes and `chezzi run` dies with `has overflowed its stack`, rc = -6** — the exact crash the gap exists to prevent. The shipped bound is on a **synthesized** measure instead: `Parser::fold_depth` carries the fold depth of the deepest subtree already built, each fold loop resets it before its children and restores `outer.max(self.fold_depth + chain)` on exit, so it `max`-combines over siblings (breadth still costs nothing — a 48 000-element list and a 48 000-argument call both parse) and *sums* up the spine (composition is caught). All **three** backtrack sites that save/restore `self.depth` restore `fold_depth` too, found by grepping `self.pos = save` rather than trusting the list. **The margin is now measured, not derived**: debug `chezzi run` survives 33 000 AST nodes and aborts at 33 500 (the derived 33 100 was right), so against the ~33 100-node derived cliff 16 000 is a **2.07×** margin (33 100/16 000 = 2.06875) and the worst accepted AST (~15 968) is also **2.07×** (33 100/15 968 = 2.0729) — same denominator, two numerators that round the same; against the measured 33 000-node cliff they diverge instead — 16 000 is **2.06×** (33 000/16 000 = 2.0625) and ~15 968 is **2.07×** (33 000/15 968 = 2.0666). **Two asserting tests, Rust by necessity** (a host `SIGABRT`, a chosen thread stack size and a parse-boundary bisection are outside what `tests/chz/` `assert` can express): `parser::tests::max_depth_boundary_accepts_then_rejects` **bisects** the boundary for all seven guarded productions and fails with the measured number (the sizing oracle — a hard-coded boundary rots into prose the moment a parser frame changes width), and `check_errors_json::worst_accepted_nesting_never_signal_crashes` drives `ast`/`check`/`run` over the worst program the parser accepts (the margin oracle — the only test that exercises both constants, both big stacks and the `cmd_ast` hop together, in the debug profile that binds). **(4) SAME-DAY FOLLOW-UP — the bound was PER-`Parser`, so it was a bound on nothing.** Every number above was enforced by the `Parser` object that builds a tree, and an interpolated `{…}` fragment is built by a **second** one: `interpolation::parse_expr_str` re-lexes the fragment text and calls `parser::parse_expr`, whose `depth`/`fold_depth` start at zero. The budgets therefore **composed**. **Measured on `e1137096`**, fixture = *L* levels of `"{ <15 985 deep> }".len()` (three DISTINCT quote styles — an alternating two-quote scheme fails to lex at level 3; every value `int` and type-clean, because a type error short-circuits before the walk that aborts; the `k` paren wraps OUTSIDE the literal, so the enclosing parser and the fragment parser each spend their own budget; `NF + K*499 = 15 485`, just under the cap, so only composition can reject): peak `desugar::walk_expr` depth **15 000 / 30 000 / 45 000** for L = 1/2/3 — exactly the sum. `chezzi check` accepted L = 3 **and** L = 4 (rc 0, ~46 000 and ~62 000 nodes against the ~33 100 cliff — it runs on the 1 GiB front-end stack) while debug `chezzi run` died **rc 134, `thread '<unknown>' has overflowed its stack / fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting`** on the 384 MiB VM worker: the uncatchable SIGABRT on a well-typed program this row exists to prevent, one enforcement point short. **The fix bounds the finished tree, not the re-parse.** The plan was to thread a remaining-budget parameter through `parse_expr_str` and have all three `parse_interpolation` consumers pass `MAX_AST_DEPTH − <own walk depth>`; measurement made that unnecessary. `desugar::Walker::walk_expr`'s `ExprKind::Str` arm parses the fragment and **re-enters its own walk on the fragment's subtree**, so a single `Walker` descends the whole composed tree — its recursion depth IS the real depth of what the checker and compiler descend next, exact rather than a per-parse estimate, one number no caller can forget to pass, and its own recursion is bounded by the same check. Every front-end path routes through it (`resolver::build_graph` ends in `desugar::run`; `chezzi run` re-does `build_graph` on the VM thread *before* `compile_graph`; `chezzi check`/`test` and the LSP all go through `build_graph`). The other three `parse_interpolation` callers — `checker::check_interpolation`, `checker::scan_expr_for_pin`, `compiler::compile_str`/`interp_exprs` — are fallbacks for an `ExprKind::Str` this walk did not convert. That is now ONLY a malformed interpolation, which re-fails at the same `parse_interpolation` and descends nothing, so none of them needs a budget of its own; the one other way in — a well-formed literal spliced by a pass-2 default this walk never reached — is the residual described below, closed by W7-51. **No over-narrowing among single-parser shapes, bisected before AND after on release binaries:** double-fold *k* = **16** (~15 968 nodes), flat fold chain **15 997**, postfix chain **15 996**, composed `f(g(…)+1×99)` **127**, parens **254** — all five unchanged, because the worst single-parse tree (15 998 nodes) is under the cap by construction. That is not "nothing that parsed before stops parsing" in general: a SIXTH shape, a default argument spliced by `normalize_call`, composes with the caller's expression exactly like an interpolated fragment and is a program the five-shape bisection never covered. Measured, release binary: `fn f(a: int = <15 000-deep chain>) -> int: return a` called as `x := f() + <2000-deep chain>` — `check` accepted it (rc 0) and `run` printed the answer on `e1137096`; HEAD refuses it with `expression nested too deeply`. What narrowed is composition — both the interpolation seam and this default-splice seam: L ≥ 2 now gets `resolve error (line 1, col 39): expression nested too deeply (limit 16000); this counts the whole expression after desugaring, and an interpolated `{…}` fragment or a spliced default argument nests INSIDE the expression around it and spends the same budget` — the enclosing context is named, because a bare `too deeply` pointing inside a fragment tells the user nothing about who ate the budget. Statement nesting cannot compose (a fragment holds an expression, never a block) and stays bounded by `MAX_DEPTH`. Pinned by `check_errors_json::composed_interp_depth_is_bounded_globally`, **Rust by necessity and verified to fail pre-fix in both profiles** (`code() == None` in debug, a missing diagnostic in release): a host SIGABRT is invisible from inside the program and a compile-time refusal is outside what `recover:` can catch, so `tests/chz/` cannot express either. **Two residual test holes closed with it.** `parser::tests::max_ast_depth_floor_holds` pinned a **15 000**-fold fixture against a real flat-chain ceiling of 15 997, so `MAX_AST_DEPTH` could have been silently cut to 15 100 with every depth test green — widened to 15 950. And `deep_iterative_chains_error_not_crash`'s "the assertion is a RATIO, so it survives any future value of `MAX_AST_DEPTH`" was false above ~50 800: each `(…)` level costs ~2 parse frames, so the single-fold bisection saturates against `MAX_DEPTH` at ~254 levels and at `MAX_AST_DEPTH = 60_000` the test goes red blaming a fold loop when the CONSTANT is what moved — it now asserts the non-saturation precondition (`MAX_AST_DEPTH / N < MAX_DEPTH / 2`) first, with a message that says which knob to turn (a `const` block, so it is a BUILD error past ~51 200, not a red run). **One residual was OPEN when this row first shipped, and is now CLOSED by W7-51 (2026-08-13) — which is why the claim above is unqualified.** Found by adversarial review of this very fix: `desugar`'s `regs` was built ONCE before both passes, so a spliced default was raw declaration AST, and `normalize_call` spliced it in the **tail** of `walk_expr_inner` — after that node's children were walked. A splice performed on **pass 2** was therefore never walked, and there was no pass 3; a default-of-a-default is exactly that shape. A well-formed interpolated literal inside one survived as `ExprKind::Str` and was re-parsed by `checker::check_interpolation` / `compiler::compile_str` with a fresh `Parser`. **Measured then**, `fn g(a: int = "{ 1+1×15990 }".len())` / `fn h(b: int = g())` / `x := h()+1×15990`: `check` rc 0, the guard's counter peaked at **15 995**, the tree the checker and compiler descend was **~31 986** nodes — a **1.03×** margin against the measured ~33 100 cliff, i.e. worse than the 1.11× correction (2) above condemns. Latent, not live, and pre-existing (accepted on `e1137096` too). **W7-51 removed both of its preconditions** — the driver is ONE pass, and a non-literal default is no longer spliced as an expression at all (it is compiled once in its defining module; the call site gets a two-node call to a provider whose body is walked as an ordinary top-level `fn`, at depth 0), while the literal class that IS still cloned both excludes any `Str` carrying `{`/`}` and is re-walked by `splice_default`. So `Walker::depth` is now an upper bound on the tree the checker and compiler descend — which is what this bound was for. **Re-verified independently on `ed4830b3`, 2026-08-13**, with a probe on `checker::check_interpolation`'s success arm (it fires exactly when a well-formed `Str` reached the checker un-converted), both binaries identical but for the probe, on the fixture above: **`925dd0f7` 1 hit / peak walk depth 15 995; `ed4830b3` 0 hits / peak 15 994**; `chezzi run` prints `15995` rc 0 on both, and on `--serial` too. **Negative control, same `ed4830b3` build with the desugar `Str → Interp` conversion disabled: 2 hits** — so the zero is a live zero, not a dead probe. `check_errors_json::composed_interp_depth_is_bounded_globally` arm (c) is retained as defence in depth: accepted or refused, it must never signal-crash. **Method lesson, now in `docs/bug-discovery.md`:** when you enforce a bound on an artifact, enumerate every writer that can still mutate it after the check, not just every reader — a tail-position mutation inside the same walk is the easiest to miss, because it does not look like a second pipeline stage. **POST-REVIEW FIX WAVE (2026-08-13) — a THIRD iterative fold loop was counted by neither depth counter, and it is pre-existing.** `parse_type_postfix` (`src/parser/mod.rs`) is a `loop` that wraps a `Type::Generic` per `?`/`!` — a left-leaning TYPE tree the front-end walkers descend — and it bumped neither `self.depth` nor `fold_depth`, so it is the same class as the two expression fold loops this row fixed and the one shape the per-production sizing oracle skips. **Measured: `fn f(x: int` + `?!` × 350 000 + `) -> int:` → `fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting` on `b1307258` AND on `dfdc7a1b`; 250 000 was accepted.** (The recursive sibling forms were already guarded — `List[` × 300 000 and `[` × 300 000 both refuse cleanly — so this was the last loop of its class.) It is now charged the same way `parse_postfix`'s loop is: `parse_type` opens the fold scope (reset before the children, `max`-combined on the way out, so sibling type arguments are breadth and cost the deepest one, not their sum) and `parse_type_postfix` sums its chain on top. A type postfix chain past `MAX_AST_DEPTH` is now a clean `type nested too deeply`. Pinned by three new cases in `parser::tests::deep_iterative_chains_error_not_crash` (over-cap refusal, under-cap acceptance, and a signature far wider than the cap), verified to fail with the guard removed. Note the fixture alternates `?!`: the lexer folds `??` into the null-coalescing token | — |

Two defects were then measured on `b1307258`, both from the same root. **Defect 1 — chains break at depth 3.** `fn c5(v: int = 5)` / `c4(v = c5())` / `c3(v = c4())` / `c2(v = c3())` / `c1(v = c2())`, called as `print(c4()); print(c3()); print(c2()); print(c1())`: `b1307258` gives **5 type errors** (`'c5' expects 1 argument(s), got 0`, `'c4' …`, `'c3' …`); HEAD and CPython both print `5` four times. **Defect 2 — a caller-side global silently supplies the wrong value across modules.** `g.chz`: `K := 7` + `fn f(x: int = K) -> int: return x`; `main.chz`: `import g` + `K := 99` + `print(g.f()); print(K)`. `b1307258` prints **`99` / `99`** — a clean `check`, both engines, and the definer's `7` nowhere in sight. No new `ExprKind`, no new opcode, no VM arm; literal defaults stay inline clones. The two-pass driver became ONE pass, which is what closed `W7-50`'s cross-task residual (see that row). **Five behaviour changes ship with it, all documented in `docs/syntax.md` §5 *Default + named arguments* and none filed as a gap:** (1) `?` cannot propagate OUT of a default — a tailored error replaces the generic `'?' used in a function that returns int`; it also WIDENS, since a `Result`-typed parameter whose default propagates INSIDE the provider (`fn f(x: int!str = Ok(getr()?.len()))`) was rejected on `b1307258` and now prints `4` / `-1`. (2) A method default declared in a module the caller does not transitively depend on **falls back to the pre-W7-51 caller-scope clone**, identically in every import order. The fallback restores the base behaviour **including its hazard**, which is named rather than papered over: the clone resolves in the caller, so `510` where the definer wrote `11` (and by name coincidence sometimes the RIGHT answer), and a name the caller cannot see is a compile error (`unknown name 'u'` in module `z`) exactly as on the base. Refusing a working, CPython-agreeing program was the larger harm; where the definer IS reachable the provider is still used, which is the common case. **THE HAZARD IS CLOSED (2026-08-13, phase 1).** The fallback described in item (2) no longer exists: the provider is reached by a **direct, call-time reference** (`Op::MakeFuncIn`, indexing `Program::providers`) instead of a synthetic import, so an out-of-closure default resolves in its definer like every other. The `510` program prints `11` (CPython prints `11`), and the ceiling — a name the caller cannot see — now COMPILES and prints `12` instead of `unknown name 'u'`. No call-ABI change was needed: `docs/future.md` §3d's premise that this "cannot be made correct" was false, because the definer's module coordinate is needed at EVALUATION time, not at the call site, and `module_objs[def.module_idx]` is how every cross-module method already resolves its home. **PHASE 2 (same day) closed the rest, and `docs/future.md` §3d is DELETED.** A defaulted fn called through a first-class function value (`f := g; f()` — `'closure' expects 1 argument(s), got 0` on `0104d57b`, now `4`) and the generic-host `Self` carve-out (measured on the phase-1 commit `cd9d609b`: the CALLER's `mkl()` ran; now the definer's) are both filled by the CALLEE, from a prologue compiled into the declaring module (`Op::JumpIfProvided` + `Proto::min_arity`, sized by the one shared predicate `ast::min_callable_params` the checker's `FnSig::min_params` also uses, so checker-accepts ⟺ compiler-can-lower by construction). **No `Value` hole sentinel and no provided-mask were needed** — a short call drops a SUFFIX, and the parser already forbids a required parameter after a defaulted one, so the only unfillable shape is a KEYWORD call supplying a later parameter while omitting an earlier callee-filled one, which is now a clear refusal rather than a silent caller-scope clone. Measured neutral on the benches (fib 1.01x, struct 1.01x, poly_method 1.00x, loop 1.01x, all within noise; no bench declares a default). **Net: no non-literal default is resolved anywhere but its declaring module, in any shape.** (3) A direct cycle (`fn f(x: int = f())`) is a compile error naming the parameter, replacing the arity cascade that the silent bounded `f(f(f()))` expansion produced — `b1307258` never ACCEPTED such a program, it reported **2 type errors**, both `'f' expects 1 argument(s), got 0` (`struct S: n: int = S().n` the same; a mutual `f`/`g` cycle, 3). (4) A cycle routed through an ordinary fn (`struct S: n: int = mk().n` with `fn mk() -> S`) is check-clean and then a clean runtime fault, `maximum call depth (10000) exceeded`, rc 1, identical on both engines — the same shape as CPython's `RecursionError`. **Known limits that are documented, not bugs** (listed so they aren't re-filed): `Iterable[T]` element
recovery does not fire for a struct with only `iter` and no `next` **in BOUND position** — bound that
one concretely (`[S: Iterable[int]]`) or annotate the parameter `Iterable[int]`, where the annotation IS
the element type and nothing has to be recovered (`syntax.md`); read-only covariance is deliberately NOT
part of the model, so `List[int]` → `Iterable[Any]` (and `Iterable[int]` → `Iterable[Any]`) is REJECTED —
a protocol existential is strictly invariant in its args, same as `List`/`Map`/a user generic struct;
`.compare()` answers the operator's verdict wherever the operator has one and only falls
back to `sort()`'s total order for NaN, so a `±0.0` pair compares Equal by the method while `sort()`
orders `-0.0 < +0.0` (`spec.md`); `--max-heap`/`--timeout` are M:N-only by design.

**Considered and DEFERRED BY DECISION, 2026-08-17** — three hidden-failure sites found by the same
stdlib audit that closed the `min`/`max` row. They are **real drift**, not known-limits, so they are
recorded here rather than struck: each is a surface break wanting its own milestone, and the decision
to defer was taken deliberately (not for lack of a fix) so that a small, reviewable branch could ship.
Deliberately **not** added to the ledger table above — that table is open *bugs to fix now*, and
adding them would misrepresent settled scope decisions as outstanding work. Promote a row if and when
one is scheduled. Ancestors measured 2026-08-17 on this box (Go 1.26, CPython 3, rustc), Chezzi on the
merged `main` binary:

| site | Chezzi | Python | Rust | Go |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ch.recv()` on a closed+drained channel | **faults** `receive on a closed channel` | — | — | `v, ok := <-ch` → `0, false`, **no panic** |
| `List.index_of(missing)` | `-1` | `list.index` **raises** `ValueError` | `iter().position` → `None` | — |
| `str.index_of(missing)` | `-1` | `str.find` → `-1` | `str::find` → `None` | — |
| `Reader.read_line()` non-UTF-8 | **faults** beside its `Option`, bytes retained, later lines still reachable via `read_bytes` | `readline()` raises `UnicodeDecodeError`, **loses the valid line before it**, and every later call returns `''` — a **silent EOF claim over data still in the file** (measured CPython 3.14.7, incl. with the bad bytes past a chunk boundary) | — | `bufio.Scanner` advances and never errors — but only because a Go `string` may hold arbitrary bytes | 

1. **`Channel.recv()` → `Option[T]`.** `Channel` is Go-lineage and Go's close protocol is
   `v, ok := <-ch`; Chezzi faults instead. `try_recv() -> Option[T]` already exists and answers `None`
   on a closed channel (measured), so the shape is available — but changing `recv`'s return type
   breaks every channel program, and Chezzi has no zero value for `T` to hand back the way Go does.
   Its own milestone.
2. **`index_of`'s `-1` sentinel → `Option[int]`.** Note the two halves differ, which the first pass
   missed: `str.index_of → -1` **is** Python-faithful (`str.find`), but **`List.index_of → -1` has no
   ancestor at all** — Python's `list.index` raises and Rust's `position` returns `None`. The
   Option-shaped sibling `List.position(pred) -> Option[int]` already exists. The list half is the
   real drift; fixing only it would split a symmetric-looking pair, which is why this wants a design
   pass rather than a patch.
3. **`Reader.read_line()` → `Result[Option[str]]`.** Today `None` means EOF and a genuine failure
   (non-UTF-8, mid-read I/O error) is a **fault sitting beside** the `Option`. `docs/stdlib.md` states
   the reason outright — *"an `Option` can't carry the error"* — which is an argument for `Result`
   wrapping the `Option`, not for a fault. Touches the whole `Reader`/`lines()` surface. **Narrowed
   2026-08-17: the CARRIER SHAPE is all that is still open — the *stickiness* half is measured and
   settled.** A re-read after the fault re-faults on the same retained bytes rather than skipping the
   bad line, and the ancestors say keep it: CPython raises **once** and then goes silent (`''` forever,
   an EOF claim over data still in the file) and additionally loses the valid line *before* the bad
   one; Go's scanner only sails past because a Go `string` may hold arbitrary bytes, which a UTF-8-
   validated Chezzi `str` cannot represent. Chezzi is the **loudest and least lossy of the three** and
   the only one where every byte stays recoverable. Making the fault non-sticky would move it *toward*
   Python's silent loss — the exact inversion `correct > silent > wrong` forbids. Full measurement and
   the "do NOT 'fix' it into a skip" note now live in `docs/stdlib.md` (§`read_line`, *"Why sticky
   rather than skip-ahead"*), `std/io.chz`, and the header of
   `tests/chz/stdlib/io_reader_carry_test.chz`.

## Session log — 2026-09-05 (bug-hunt wave 10: 26 confirmed findings, W10-1..W10-26, filed as TICKET-060..069)

**Shape of the pass.** Six agents over the same disjoint domains as wave 9 (airlock/capture/generators,
cancel/defer/recover + sync primitives, checker⊋compiler, core-vs-CPython, stdlib, FFI/modules/CLI/test
runner), ~400 probe programs; every candidate re-run by the main loop on the release binary at
`CHEZZI_THREADS=1` and default before filing. 30 candidates → 26 confirmed, 2 documented-by-design
(the airlock install rule, `concurrency.md:1428`; wave-9's own decision), 2 left as decisions (a fn body
reading a `:=` global declared below it; `1 < x < 3` chaining). The `--serial` oracle the hunt prompt
still names is gone (2026-08-16): the oracles were the two-worker-count diff plus a RUN Go/Python/Rust
reference, exactly as wave 9.

**Where the 26 came from.** Domains wave 9 called clean produced most of them, from COMBINATIONS wave 9
did not try: a channel op *inside* a native re-entry *in the main task* (W10-1), a fault *while the
owner* is parked (W10-16), a guard-waiter *plus* a channel park (W10-15), a pointer *into* an argument
(W10-6), an alias *in a pattern* (W10-4), a `None` binding *written after* a typed read (W10-5 — the
exact write shape W8-46's read-only measurement did not cover). One P0 is memory-unsafe from
check-clean code (W10-6). Five are the test runner silently reporting PASS or losing a diagnostic
(W10-9..W10-12) — none reachable by a gate that reads exit codes. Two are quadratic stdlib paths
(W10-22), the W8-34 class again, found by timing, not by assertion.

**Tickets.** Related rows were bundled by seam: 060 (cffi runtime: W10-6, W10-8), 061 (FFI surface:
W10-7, W10-14), 062 (scheduler verdicts: W10-16, W10-1), 063 (guard-park hang + test wall clock:
W10-15), 064 (checker soundness: W10-5), 065 (checker false-rejects: W10-2, W10-4), 066 (parser/desugar:
W10-3, W10-17, W10-20), 067 (test runner + `--errors=json`: W10-9..13), 068 (quadratic builders:
W10-22), 069 (stdlib contracts: W10-18, W10-21, W10-23..26). W10-19 was documented in place. The
